11.01.title: What is a fluid
11.01.html:
Push a block of rubber sideways and it deforms a little, then stops: it resists shear with a stress that depends on how far you’ve pushed. Push the surface of the Limmat and the water keeps moving as long as you push. A fluid is a material that deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small. What it resists isn’t the amount of deformation but its rate, and the property measuring that resistance is viscosity.

The continuum

Water is made of molecules, but a cubic micrometre still holds about 3×1010 of them. So we treat velocity, pressure and density as smooth fields u(x,t), p(x,t), ρ(x,t). That’s the continuum hypothesis. It fails only when the flow’s length scale approaches the mean free path, as in rarefied gas at high altitude or nanochannels.

Newton’s law of viscosity

Put fluid between two parallel plates a gap h apart, fix the bottom one and slide the top one at speed U. The fluid sticks to both walls (the no-slip condition), and the shear stress needed is

τ=μdydu​.

μ is the dynamic viscosity in Pa s: about 1.0×10−3 for water at 20 °C, 1.8×10−5 for air, 0.29 for SAE 30 oil and around 10 for honey. The kinematic viscosity ν=μ/ρ, in m²/s, appears whenever inertia competes with friction. Fluids obeying this linear law are Newtonian. Ketchup, paint, blood and toothpaste aren’t.

Couette flow

With no pressure gradient, the momentum balance on a thin slab of fluid reduces to μd2u/dy2=0, so the velocity is linear:

u(y)=Uhy​,τ=μhU​ everywhere.

Add a pressure gradient and the equation becomes μu′′=dp/dx, which adds a parabola. This is the basis of lubrication: a thin oil film in a bearing carries the load while shearing at enormous rates.

Worked exampleShearing a thin film

Top plate at 2 m/s, gap 1 mm, plate area 0.5 m².

  1. Water: τ=10−3⋅2/0.001=2.0 Pa, a force of 1.0 N.
  2. SAE 30 oil: 580 Pa, 290 N. Honey: 20 000 Pa, 10 kN.
  3. The finite-difference solution of μu′′=0 is linear to machine precision, with a constant shear rate of 2000 s⁻¹.
  4. With dp/dx=−2 MPa/m in the oil, the centre speed rises from 1.0 to 1.8621 m/s. The flow rate per metre width goes from 1.0000 to 1.5745 L/s (exact: 1.5747).

Exercise 1A journal bearing

A 50 mm shaft turns at 3000 rpm in a 40 mm long bearing with a radial clearance of 0.05 mm, filled with oil of μ=0.03 Pa s. Treating the thin film as Couette flow, find the friction torque and the power lost.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Surface speed U=πDn/60=π⋅0.05⋅3000/60=7.854 m/s.
  2. Shear stress τ=0.03⋅7.854/(5×10−5)=4712 Pa.
  3. Wetted area πDL=6.283×10−3 m², so the friction force is 29.61 N.
  4. Torque 29.61⋅0.025=0.740 N m; power Tω=0.740⋅314.16=232.5 W, which ends up as heat in the oil. This is Petroff’s equation.

Shear stress (Pa) in water (μ = 1.0e-3) between plates 0.5 mm apart, top at 3 m/s. 1 decimal.
Kinematic viscosity (m²/s) of SAE 30 oil, μ = 0.29 Pa s, ρ = 880 kg/m³. 4 significant figures, e.g. 1.234e-4.
A fluid differs from a solid in that it:
options: Deforms continuously under any shear stress

11.02.title: Fluid statics
11.02.html:
Dive to the bottom of a pool and your ears hurt; drive up to the Jungfraujoch and a sealed crisp packet puffs up. Both come from one equation. In a fluid at rest there’s no shear stress, only pressure, and the pressure at a point is the same in every direction. It changes with height because each layer has to hold up the weight of everything above it.

The hydrostatic equation

Balance the forces on a small fluid element of height dz: the pressure difference across it carries its weight, so

dzdp​=−ρg.

For a liquid, ρ is constant and p=p0​+ρgh at depth h below a free surface at p0​. Ten metres of water adds 1000⋅9.81⋅10=98.1 kPa, about one atmosphere. Engineers often quote gauge pressure, measured relative to the local atmosphere, rather than absolute pressure.

For a gas, density depends on pressure: ρ=p/(RT). With the standard atmosphere’s temperature falling 6.5 K per km, integration gives p=p0​(T/T0​)g/(Rλ). Pressure falls by about 12 % per kilometre near the ground.

Manometers

A U-tube holding a dense liquid measures a pressure difference by the height difference h it supports. Walking down one leg and up the other, adding ρgΔz going down and subtracting going up,

p1​−p2​=(ρm​−ρf​)gh,

where ρm​ is the manometer fluid and ρf​ the fluid in the pipe above it. Mercury gives compact readings for large differences; water or oil gives sensitivity for small ones.

Worked exampleWater, air and mercury

  1. Gauge pressure at 10 m depth: 98.10 kPa, from integrating dp/dz=−ρg numerically.
  2. Standard atmosphere, integrated with the 6.5 K/km lapse rate: 965.2 hPa in Zurich (408 m) and 661.4 hPa on the Jungfraujoch (3454 m). The numerical integration matches the closed form to within 1 Pa.
  3. At 661.4 hPa water boils at 88.5 °C (Antoine equation), so pasta cooks slowly up there.
  4. A mercury manometer under water reading 120 mm: (13546−998)⋅9.81⋅0.120=14.772 kPa.

Exercise 1The bottom of Lake Zurich

Lake Zurich is 136 m deep at its deepest. Find the gauge and absolute pressure there, taking 96.52 kPa for atmospheric pressure at the lake surface. Then find the pressure difference read by a water manometer showing 50 mm across a fan duct carrying air (ρ=1.2 kg/m³).

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Gauge: 1000⋅9.81⋅136=1.334 MPa, about 13 atmospheres.
  2. Absolute: 1.334+0.0965=1.431 MPa.
  3. Manometer: (998−1.2)⋅9.81⋅0.050=488.9 Pa. Air’s density barely matters here.

quiz.q: Gauge pressure (kPa) at 136 m depth in fresh water (ρ = 1000). 2 decimals.
Δp (kPa) for a 200 mm mercury reading under water (ρ_m 13 546, ρ_f 998). 3 decimals.
Depth (m) of fresh water that adds one standard atmosphere (101.325 kPa). 3 decimals.
In a fluid at rest the pressure at a point:
options: Is the same in all directions

quiz.q: Why does a crisp packet puff up on the Jungfraujoch?
quiz.explain: Sealed at about 965 hPa, now at 661 hPa.
options: Outside pressure is about a third lower

11.03.title: Buoyancy and stability
11.03.html:
A coconut that falls into a Bali river floats away, sometimes across oceans; that’s how coconut palms spread around the tropics. A ship loaded with containers stays upright in waves, until someone stacks them too high. Both are hydrostatics. Floating is about the size of the buoyant force; staying upright is about where it acts.

Archimedes

The pressure on a submerged body is higher underneath than on top. Adding it up over the surface gives an upward force equal to the weight of displaced fluid:

FB​=ρf​gVsub​.

It acts at the centre of buoyancy B, the centroid of the displaced volume. A floating body sinks until FB​ equals its weight, so the submerged fraction is ρbody​/ρf​. A husked coconut of 1.2 kg and 1.9 litres floats 63 % submerged in fresh water.

Stability and the metacentre

Heel a floating hull by a small angle θ. Its weight still acts at the centre of gravity G, but the underwater shape changes: one side goes deeper, the other rises, and B moves towards the low side. The vertical through the new B crosses the centreline at the metacentre M. If M is above G, weight and buoyancy form a couple that pushes the hull back upright.

The height of M above B is

BM=VIwp​​,

where Iwp​ is the second moment of area of the waterplane about the roll axis and V is the displaced volume. For a box barge of beam B and draft T, BM=B2/(12T). The metacentric height is

GM=KB+BM−KG,

measured from the keel K. The hull is stable if and only if GM>0, and for small heel the righting arm is GZ≈GMsinθ. Wide hulls are stable; high loads aren’t.

Worked exampleA box barge

A barge 20 m long, 6 m beam and 2.5 m deep displaces 150 t in seawater (ρ=1025 kg/m³), with KG=1.8 m.

  1. Draft T=150000/(1025⋅20⋅6)=1.2195 m; KB=0.6098 m; BM=36/(12⋅1.2195)=2.4600 m.
  2. GM=0.6098+2.4600−1.8=1.2698 m: stable.
  3. The code finds GZ by clipping the hull polygon at a tilted waterline that keeps the displaced area constant. At 1° GZ = 0.0222 m, exactly GMsinθ; at 10° it’s 0.2271 m against 0.2205, matching the wall-sided formula GZ=sinθ(GM+21​BMtan2θ).
  4. Raising KG to 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 and 4.0 m gives GM of +2.070, +1.070, +0.070 and −0.930 m. The last one capsizes, and the sign of GZ always matches the sign of GM.

Exercise 1Deck cargo

The barge above must keep GM≥0.5 m for safety. What’s the highest allowed centre of gravity, at the same displacement?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. KGmax​=KB+BM−0.5=0.6098+2.4600−0.5=2.5698 m.
  2. The deck is 2.5 m above the keel, so the combined centre of gravity of barge and cargo may sit only about 7 cm above deck level. Heavy deck cargo must be balanced by low ballast.

Draft (m) of a 20 × 6 m barge of 150 t in seawater (1025 kg/m³). 4 decimals.
Submerged fraction of a coconut of 1.2 kg and 1.9 L in fresh water. 4 decimals.

11.04.title: Flow kinematics
11.04.html:
Before asking what forces drive a flow, we need ways to describe the motion itself. Drop a coconut into the Limmat and follow it, or stand on a bridge and watch the water passing one spot. Those are the two viewpoints of fluid mechanics. Then there are three different “lines” you can draw through a flow, and they only agree when nothing changes in time.

Lagrangian and Eulerian descriptions

  • Lagrangian: follow individual fluid particles, xp​(t). Natural for a coconut, a drifting buoy or a smoke particle.
  • Eulerian: describe the velocity at every fixed point, u(x,t). Natural for measurements at a bridge pier, and what almost all fluid equations use.

The link is dxp​/dt=u(xp​,t): integrating the Eulerian field gives particle paths.

Three kinds of line

  • A streamline is everywhere tangent to the velocity at one instant: dx/ds∥u(x,t0​) with time frozen.
  • A pathline is the trajectory of one particle over time.
  • A streakline joins all particles that passed through one fixed point, like dye from a nozzle or smoke from a chimney.

In steady flow the field doesn’t change, so a particle simply runs along its streamline and all three coincide. In unsteady flow they differ, sometimes dramatically. A smoke trail in gusty wind is a streakline, and it doesn’t show you where the air is going now.

A worked field

Take u=U0​, v=V0​sinωt: uniform in space, but the cross-flow oscillates. At any instant the streamlines are straight parallel lines with slope V0​sin(ωt)/U0​. A particle released at the origin at t=0 follows x=U0​t, y=V0​(1−cosωt)/ω, a wave entirely above the axis. The streakline at t=2π/ω is the mirror image, entirely below.

Worked exampleTracing with RK4

U0​=1 m/s, V0​=0.5 m/s, ω=1 rad/s.

  1. Pathline from the origin over one period: it ends at (6.2832, 0) and peaks at y=1.0000=2V0​/ω, as the exact solution says.
  2. Streamline at t=π/2: straight with slope 0.5000 =V0​/U0​.
  3. Streakline at t=2π: y from −1.0000 to 0, the mirror image of the pathline.
  4. For a steady field u=1, v=0.3, all three lines lie on y=0.3x to machine precision.

Exercise 1One more particle

In the same field, where is a particle released from the origin at t0​=π when t=2π? Is that point on the pathline of the particle released at t=0, on the streakline at t=2π, or both?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. x=U0​(t−t0​)=π=3.1416 m.
  2. y=V0​(cosωt0​−cosωt)/ω=0.5(cosπ−cos2π)=−1.0 m.
  3. It’s on the streakline at 2π (all particles from the origin, by definition), at its lowest point. The pathline from t=0 at x=π is at y=+1.0, so the point isn’t on that pathline.

Streamline slope at t = π/6 with U₀ = 1, V₀ = 0.5, ω = 1. 2 decimals.
y (m) at t = 2π of the particle released at t₀ = π/2 (V₀ = 0.5, ω = 1). 2 decimals.

11.05.title: The material derivative
11.05.html:
Water flowing steadily through a nozzle speeds up as the nozzle narrows. At every fixed point nothing changes in time, yet each parcel of water accelerates, and Newton’s second law is about parcels. The material derivative is the bridge: the rate of change seen by someone riding with the fluid, written in Eulerian variables.

Following a parcel

Let q(x,t) be any field: temperature, a velocity component, a dye concentration. A parcel at xp​(t) sees q(xp​(t),t), and by the chain rule

DtDq​=∂t∂q​+u∂x∂q​+v∂y∂q​+w∂z∂q​=∂t∂q​+(u⋅∇)q.

The first term is the local change at a fixed point; the second is the convective change from moving to a place where q is different. Applied to velocity it gives the acceleration of a fluid particle:

a=DtDu​=∂t∂u​+(u⋅∇)u.

The convective term is nonlinear in u. That’s the source of most of the difficulty, and the richness, of fluid mechanics, turbulence included.

Two examples

  • Stagnation-point flow u=ax, v=−ay, like water hitting a wall: steady, yet a=(a2x,a2y). Parcels accelerate away from the wall along it and decelerate as they approach.
  • Solid-body rotation u=−Ωy, v=Ωx: steady, and a=−Ω2(x,y), the centripetal acceleration of circular motion.

Worked exampleA strengthening stagnation flow

u=a(t)x, v=−a(t)y with a=0.5(1+0.2t) s⁻¹, at (2, 1) m and t=3 s.

  1. Local acceleration (central differences in time): (0.2, −0.1) m/s².
  2. Convective: (1.28, 0.64) m/s². Total (1.48, 0.54), matching the exact (a˙x+a2x, −a˙y+a2y).
  3. Following the exact particle path and differentiating its velocity gives the same (1.48, 0.54).
  4. With a constant at 0.5, the local part vanishes but the convective acceleration at (2, 1) is still (0.5, 0.25) m/s².

Exercise 1A nozzle

In a nozzle the centreline speed is u=U0​(1+x/L) with U0​=2 m/s and L=0.5 m. Find the acceleration of a water parcel at x=0.25 m. Then let the supply ramp up so that U0​=2+t (m/s, t in s) and find it again at t=0.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. u=2(1+0.5)=3 m/s and ∂u/∂x=U0​/L=4 s⁻¹.
  2. Steady: a=u∂u/∂x=3⋅4=12 m/s², over a g, with nothing changing in time.
  3. Ramping: the local term is U˙0​(1+x/L)=1⋅1.5=1.5 m/s², so a=13.5 m/s².

quiz.q: Steady acceleration (m/s²) in the nozzle at x = 0.5 m (U₀ = 2, L = 0.5).
Centripetal acceleration magnitude (m/s²) at r = 2 m in solid-body rotation with Ω = 0.5 rad/s. 2 decimals.
Convective x-acceleration (m/s²) in u = ax, v = −ay with a = 0.8 s⁻¹ at x = 3 m. 2 decimals.
In steady flow, the material acceleration is:
options: The convective term (u·∇)u, which can be non-zero

quiz.q: Which term makes the Navier-Stokes equations nonlinear?

11.06.title: Conservation of mass
11.06.html:
Put your thumb over the end of a garden hose and the water shoots out faster. No water is created or destroyed, so what goes in must come out: squeeze the area and the speed goes up. That’s continuity, the first of the conservation laws, written once for a control volume and once for every point of the flow.

The Reynolds transport theorem

Physical laws are written for a fixed lump of matter (a system). Engineers prefer a fixed region of space, a control volume (CV), that fluid flows through. The Reynolds transport theorem links them: for any extensive property B with intensity β=B/m,

dtdBsys​​=dtd​∫CV​ρβdV+∮CS​ρβ(u⋅n)dA.

Rate of change of the system = accumulation inside + net outflow through the surface. With B = mass, β=1 and the left side is zero.

Integral and differential forms

For steady flow, mass flow in equals mass flow out: ∑m˙in​=∑m˙out​. For an incompressible fluid in a pipe,

Q=A1​V1​=A2​V2​,

with V the mean speed. Halve a pipe’s diameter and the speed quadruples.

Shrinking the control volume to a point with Gauss’s theorem gives

∂t∂ρ​+∇⋅(ρu)=0⇒∇⋅u=∂x∂u​+∂y∂v​+∂z∂w​=0

for incompressible flow. Any velocity field you invent must satisfy this to be physically possible, and CFD codes spend much of their effort enforcing it.

Worked exampleChecking fields and pipes

  1. On an 81 × 81 grid, the stagnation flow (x,−y) and the vortex (−y,x) have zero divergence (to 10−15) and zero net outflow through the boundary square.
  2. The expanding field (x,y) has divergence 2 everywhere and net outflow 8.0000 through the 2 × 2 square, equal to divergence × area, as Gauss requires. It can’t be an incompressible flow.
  3. A water main carrying 70 L/s: 0.990 m/s in the 300 mm section, 3.961 m/s in the 150 mm throat, 2.228 m/s in the 200 mm section, 70.0 L/s through each.

Exercise 1The thumb on the hose

A 16 mm garden hose delivers 0.3 L/s. A nozzle narrows the outlet to 5 mm. Find the speed in the hose and at the nozzle.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Hose area π⋅0.0162/4=2.011×10−4 m², so V1​=0.0003/2.011×10−4=1.492 m/s.
  2. Nozzle: V2​=V1​(16/5)2=1.492⋅10.24=15.28 m/s, fast enough to reach several metres. In reality the pump or mains pressure may not keep the flow rate constant when you restrict the outlet; that needs the energy equation (next lesson).

quiz.q: Nozzle speed (m/s) for 0.3 L/s through a 5 mm hole. 2 decimals.
Speed ratio when a pipe’s diameter goes from 300 to 100 mm.
Divergence of u = 3x, v = −y, w = −2z.
For incompressible flow, continuity says:
Which field is impossible for an incompressible fluid?

11.07.title: Bernoulli's equation
11.07.html:
Bernoulli’s equation is the most used and most misused result in fluid mechanics. It explains why a venturi meter measures flow, why a garden sprayer sucks up fertiliser, and why the pressure drops where a river speeds up between bridge piers. It also gets quoted for things it doesn’t explain. To use it properly, derive it and keep the assumptions in view.

Derivation along a streamline

Apply Newton’s second law to a fluid particle moving along a streamline, with coordinate s. Ignoring viscosity, the only forces are pressure and gravity:

ρ(∂t∂V​+V∂s∂V​)=−∂s∂p​−ρg∂s∂z​.

For steady, incompressible flow, V∂V/∂s=∂(V2/2)/∂s, and integrating along the streamline gives

p+21​ρV2+ρgz=constant along a streamline.

The terms are static pressure, dynamic pressure and hydrostatic pressure. Divided by ρg they become heads in metres.

When it lies

The assumptions: steady, incompressible (Mach number below about 0.3), inviscid (no friction losses), and along one streamline. The constant can differ between streamlines unless the flow is also irrotational. It fails across pumps or turbines (they add or remove energy), in long pipes (friction), in separated wakes, and through hydraulic jumps. The popular “equal transit time” explanation of wing lift is not Bernoulli; it’s just wrong.

The venturi meter

Combining Bernoulli with continuity, V1​A1​=V2​A2​, between an inlet of diameter D and a throat of diameter d gives

Q=Cd​A2​ρ(1−β4)2Δp​​,β=Dd​.

The discharge coefficient Cd​≈0.98 absorbs the small friction losses.

Worked exampleA 100/50 mm venturi

  1. A mercury manometer under water reads 150 mm, so Δp=(13546−998)⋅9.81⋅0.150=18.464 kPa.
  2. Throat area A2​=1.9635×10−3 m² and β4=0.0625, so the ideal throat speed is 2⋅18464/(998⋅0.9375)​=6.282 m/s and Q=0.98⋅A2​⋅6.282=12.089 L/s (ideal 12.336).
  3. Integrating the 1D Euler equation ρudu/dx=−dp/dx along a smooth contraction carrying the ideal flow gives a pressure drop of 18.4644 kPa: the same as Bernoulli and the manometer.
  4. Speed rises from 1.571 m/s at the inlet to 6.282 m/s in the throat.

Exercise 1What will the manometer read?

The same venturi will carry 10 L/s of water. What mercury manometer reading should you expect (ideal flow)?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. V1​=0.01/(π⋅0.12/4)=1.273 m/s; V2​=4V1​=5.093 m/s.
  2. Δp=21​⋅998⋅(5.0932−1.2732)=12.134 kPa.
  3. h=12134/((13546−998)⋅9.81)=98.6 mm of mercury.

quiz.q: Manometer reading (mm Hg) for 10 L/s in the 100/50 mm venturi. 1 decimal.
Dynamic pressure (Pa) of water at 3 m/s. 0 decimals.
Speed (m/s) of water from a hole 2 m below a free surface (ideal). 3 decimals.

11.08.title: Torricelli and draining tanks
11.08.html:
How long does a rain-water tank take to empty through its tap? When will a leaking reservoir drop to half? In 1643 Evangelista Torricelli found that water leaves a hole at the speed a stone would reach falling from the free surface. Combined with conservation of mass, that gives a differential equation for the level, and a result that surprises most people: the second half of the water takes much longer than the first.

Torricelli’s law

Apply Bernoulli from the free surface (pressure atmospheric, speed nearly zero, height h above the hole) to the jet (atmospheric, speed V, height 0):

V=2gh​.

Real jets contract just outside a sharp-edged hole (the vena contracta) and lose a little to friction. The discharge coefficient Cd​≈0.61 for a sharp orifice accounts for both, so Q=Cd​a2gh​.

The draining equation

If the level falls slowly, the flow is quasi-steady: at each instant Torricelli holds with the current h. Mass conservation for a tank of cross-section A(h):

A(h)dtdh​=−Cd​a2gh​.

For a constant-area tank, separating variables gives h​=h0​​−2ACd​a​2g​t, and the time to empty is

tempty​=Cd​aA​g2h0​​​.

Because the outflow slows as h​, the bottom half of a cylinder takes 2​+1≈2.4 times as long as the top half. For other shapes, integrate numerically.

Worked exampleA rain-water tank

1.2 m diameter, 1.5 m of water, 25 mm sharp-edged outlet, Cd​=0.61.

  1. Initial outflow speed 2⋅9.81⋅1.5​=5.425 m/s; flow 1.624 L/s.
  2. Time to empty: 2088.7 s (34.81 min) from the closed form; RK4 gives 2088.7 s.
  3. The top half drains in 611.8 s, the bottom half in 1476.9 s.
  4. An inverted cone of the same top and height holds a third as much water and empties in 417.8 s by RK4 (exact 417.7), 0.20 of the cylinder’s time.

Exercise 1A bigger tap

Replace the 25 mm outlet with a 50 mm one. How long does the full tank take to empty, and how long to fall from 1.5 m to 0.5 m?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The hole area quadruples, so the time falls by 4: 34.81/4=8.70 min.
  2. From 1.5 to 0.5 m: t=Cd​aA​2g​2​(1.5​−0.5​)=3.68 min. Two thirds of the water leaves in 42 % of the total time.

quiz.q: Time (min) to empty the 1.2 m tank from 1.5 m through a 50 mm hole (C_d 0.61). 2 decimals.
Ratio of the bottom-half to top-half draining time of a cylinder. 4 decimals.
Flow (L/s) from a 20 mm sharp orifice under 3 m head, C_d = 0.61. 4 decimals.
Why does the outflow slow down as the tank drains?
options: The driving head h falls, and V ∝ √h

quiz.q: The quasi-steady assumption means:
options: At each instant the steady Torricelli law holds with the current h

11.09.title: The momentum theorem
11.09.html:
A fire hose bucks in your hands; a pipe bend in a hydropower plant needs a concrete anchor block weighing tonnes; a jet of water knocks a plate backwards. You don’t need to know the details of the flow inside to get those forces. Draw a control volume around the device and count the momentum going in and out.

The control-volume momentum balance

Apply the Reynolds transport theorem to momentum: the sum of forces on the fluid in a fixed control volume equals the rate of change of momentum inside plus the net momentum outflow. For steady flow with uniform inlets and outlets,

∑F=out∑​m˙V−in∑​m˙V.

The forces include pressure on the inlet and outlet faces (pA, pushing inwards), the force from the walls, and gravity. It’s a vector equation, so work component by component, and draw the control volume first.

Jets on vanes

A free jet is at atmospheric pressure everywhere, so only the vane pushes on it. A jet of mass flow m˙ and speed V turned by an angle θ pushes the vane with

Fx​=m˙V(1−cosθ).

A flat plate (θ=90°) feels m˙V; turning the jet right back (180°) doubles it.

Pipe bends

In a pipe the pressure terms usually dominate. For a horizontal bend turning the flow by θ, the force the fluid puts on the bend (and the anchor must resist) is

F=(p1​A1​+m˙V1​)e1​−(p2​A2​+m˙V2​)e2​,

where e1​ and e2​ are the inlet and outlet flow directions.

Worked exampleJets and a bend

  1. Water jet, 30 mm at 20 m/s: m˙=14.109 kg/s. Force on a vane turning it 90°: 282.2 N; 135°: 481.7 N; 180°: 564.4 N, exactly 2m˙V.
  2. 90° reducing bend, 200 L/s, 300 → 200 mm, inlet 150 kPa gauge. V1​=2.829 m/s, V2​=6.366 m/s, p2​=133.77 kPa by Bernoulli.
  3. Force on the bend: Fx​=11168 N, Fy​=−5473 N, magnitude 12 437 N, about 1.3 tonnes, mostly from pressure.
  4. With the flow stopped, only pressure acts: pA along both axes, which the code checks.

Exercise 1A fire nozzle

A fire hose of 65 mm diameter ends in a 25 mm nozzle discharging 10 L/s to the atmosphere. Find the gauge pressure at the nozzle inlet (Bernoulli) and the force in the coupling that holds the nozzle onto the hose.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. V1​=0.01/(π⋅0.0652/4)=3.014 m/s; V2​=20.37 m/s.
  2. p1​=21​⋅998⋅(20.372−3.0142)=202.6 kPa gauge.
  3. Momentum on the nozzle’s fluid, along the axis: Fnozzle on fluid​+p1​A1​=m˙(V2​−V1​), so F=9.98⋅17.36−202559⋅3.318×10−3=173.3−672.2=−498.9 N.
  4. The fluid pushes the nozzle forward with 498.9 N, and the coupling must carry that in tension. The firefighter feels the jet reaction m˙V2​=203 N.
